design_detail: Narrative review by three Australian authors (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2010;107:1-10), read as the published PDF; page numbers are the journal's own (pp. 1-10). It asks whether there is evidence for an ecstasy (MDMA) dependence syndrome. Searches were run in PubMed, PsycInfo and EMBASE with the strings given in footnote 1 (p. 2), but no dates, inclusion or exclusion rules or numbers of records are stated. Structure: theory of dependence and the DSM-IV and ICD-10 classifications (pp. 2-3); animal evidence with pure MDMA (pp. 3-6); human evidence (pp. 6-8): three case reports (Jansen, 1999; p. 6), 14 survey samples in Table 1 (pp. 4-6; editors' count: 3 population-based, 2 sentinel populations, 9 self-selected samples, with sample sizes from 26 to 1,662 and reported prevalence from 3.6% to 73%), the structure of the dependence criteria (p. 7), course, treatment seeking and limitations (p. 8), and a summary (p. 8). The authors state that the studies differ too much in method and sample for a meta-analysis (3.6, p. 8). No effect sizes are pooled and no intervals are given.
can_establish: What studies published up to 2009 found when they asked people who take ecstasy about dependence symptoms, as summarized by three authors: the range of reported prevalence by type of sample, the symptoms most often endorsed, that the dependence reported was often not persistent (one German cohort: 93% no longer dependent after about three years), and that treatment for ecstasy alone was uncommon in Australian records (under 1% of episodes).
cannot_establish: How common dependence on MDMA is in any defined group of people. The prevalence figures come from different instruments (DSM-IV hallucinogen, amphetamine or stimulant criteria, the Severity of Dependence Scale at different cut-offs, a screener, a clinician interview), different time windows (lifetime, past year, past month) and mostly self-selected samples, and pills sold as ecstasy may contain methamphetamine (p. 3), so some of the dependence reported may not be on MDMA. It cannot show that tolerance and withdrawal reported on questionnaires reflect changes in the brain rather than the after-effects of a recent session, or what would happen to people followed from first use.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable to the review itself. In the 14 samples of Table 1 (pp. 4-6): three came from household or population surveys of young adults (Stone; von Sydow; Wu), two from sentinel populations (New York nightclub attendees; Taiwanese juvenile detainees), and nine were self-selected (purposive or snowball sampling, rave attendees, readers of a dance magazine, people in treatment services and students).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search strings in three databases are given (footnote 1, p. 2). No dates, inclusion or exclusion criteria or counts are given, and the review also draws on government statistics, a monograph and a case-report series (Jansen, 1999).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (narrative review). Table 1 rows range from adolescents and young adults to heavy-using rave attendees.
sample.selection_effects: Stated by the review: most studies recruited people who had recently taken ecstasy by convenience or snowball sampling, so the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to everyone taking ecstasy (3.6, p. 8). Editors' observations: the highest figures come from small samples selected for heavy use or drawn partly from treatment services (Cottler, 52 people; Thomasius, 59 people with at least 250 lifetime tablets); the lowest come from household surveys, where the question was about hallucinogen dependence criteria; the review does not say how it chose which studies to put in Table 1.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported ecstasy use. No study in Table 1 verified by laboratory test what people had taken (p. 3). Dependence was measured with questionnaires or interviews built for other drugs: the CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale, DSM-IV hallucinogen items, amphetamine-dependence questions from a children's interview schedule, a three-item arrestee screener and, in one non-representative sample, a clinician-rated SCID interview (Thomasius; p. 6).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Lifetime use was reported as means of about 160 occasions (Winstock), 227 pills (Scheier) and 794 tablets (Thomasius, a sample chosen for at least 250 tablets); use in the preceding weeks or months was a median of 2.5 days (Parsons, window as printed) and 12 days in the past six months (range 2-100; Topp, 1997; Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Not controlled in most samples. Where studies adjusted for other drug use, including methamphetamine (Bruno et al., 2009; Topp et al., 1997), they used self-reported use, not laboratory-verified use (p. 3). Thomasius reports high polydrug use (cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine, LSD) and Tossman's sample was people using ecstasy and/or methamphetamine (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Mostly none. The few comparisons in Table 1 and the text are: ecstasy against LSD, peyote and psilocybin for hallucinogen dependence (Stone), people screening positive against negative (Bruno; Parsons, with median days of use 5 against 2 in the past four weeks) and one German cohort followed for just over three years (von Sydow; p. 8).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed as a limit of the evidence. Scheier found lifetime ecstasy use, motivational factors, criminal behaviour and depression to be independent predictors of dependence (p. 7), so what came before the ecstasy use is not separated from the use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Adjusted by self-reported other drug use in two studies (Topp, 1997; Bruno, 2009); not adjusted in the others reported.

outcomes.instruments: CIDI (computerised and modified versions), Severity of Dependence Scale (cut-offs of 4 and 5), DSM-IV hallucinogen items, amphetamine-dependence questions (Yen and Hsu), the Center for Substance Abuse Research arrestee screener, SCID (clinician-rated).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes that all the instruments were first designed for other drugs, and that the Severity of Dependence Scale has shown good reliability and validity for opioids, cocaine and amphetamines, where it is unidimensional, whereas for ecstasy it did not have a single factor (p. 7). Topp and colleagues questioned the validity of the withdrawal items (p. 6), and the review says it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as intended (3.6, p. 8).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Dependence' differs between studies: DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence (Stone; Wu), CIDI ecstasy, hallucinogen and stimulant dependence (von Sydow), Severity of Dependence Scale at 4 or more (Bruno) or 5 or more (Winstock), amphetamine-dependence questions (Yen and Hsu), a three-item 'probable' screener (Yacoubian), latent classes of symptoms (Scheier), clinician SCID (Thomasius). Windows differ too: lifetime, past year, past month, or not specified (Table 1, p. 6, footnote a).

analysis.effect_sizes: Prevalence of dependence as reported in Table 1 (pp. 4-6), with no intervals. Population-based samples: 3.8% past year (Stone, 1,199 people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years; hallucinogen criteria), 5.8% lifetime among those who had ever taken ecstasy (von Sydow, 207 young adults), 3.6% past year (Wu, 652; the text gives 4%). Sentinel populations: 19% past year (Parsons, 214 nightclub attendees), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, 200 detainees). Self-selected samples: 18% past month (Bruno, 1,662, Severity of Dependence Scale 4 or more), 43% lifetime (Cottler, 52), 64% lifetime (Topp 1997, 185), 16% (Tossman, 195, past-year ecstasy and/or methamphetamine; window not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, 154, 'probable' on a screener), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, 59 people with at least 250 lifetime tablets), 17% (Winstock, 1,106; window not specified in Table 1, lifetime in the text). Hanson and Luciana (26): 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the text, where Table 1 prints 'N = 2 LT'. Scheier (639): latent classes, no prevalence in the table. Text, p. 7: past-year dependence among all young adults in Germany 0.4% (von Sydow). Course, p. 8: of the people classified as dependent at the start, 93% were no longer dependent after a mean of just over three years; 50% no longer used at all; most of the 43% still using no longer met criteria. Treatment, p. 8: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable to the review; adjustment for other drugs in the cited studies was by self-report.
analysis.selective_reporting: No selection rule beyond the search strings. The review gives different quantities for different studies (lifetime, past year, 'probable', latent-class share) and does not put them on a common scale; the figure for one row (Thomasius, 73%) is in Table 1 only, and the figure of 73% in the text belongs to Scheier's latent classes.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 14 samples that used instruments built for other drugs, the share screening positive for dependence ranged from 3.6% to 73%. About 4 in 100 came from household surveys asking about the past year; 16 to 22 in 100 from nightclub attendees, detainees and regular-use samples; 43 to 73 in 100 from small samples selected for heavy use or including people in treatment. In the one cohort followed, 93% of those classified as dependent no longer were after about three years. Tolerance and withdrawal rest on self-report on questionnaires designed for other drugs; pills sold as ecstasy may contain methamphetamine; case reports are few (three) and mild.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says the evidence is limited in both scope and design and that further controlled work is needed (p. 8), which matches the content. Two statements go further than the data: the abstract's 'Human evidence supports this proposition' (physical features playing a more limited role than psychological ones) rests partly on the absence of case reports of severe withdrawal, and on questionnaire items from other drugs; and the two-factor structure ('compulsive use' and 'escalating use') is proposed from two studies, both by the review's own authors and both in Australia (p. 7).

timeline.event: Australian sample of 185 regular ecstasy-taking people: 64% met CIDI lifetime criteria, typically in their heaviest period, and the authors questioned the withdrawal items (Topp et al.; as summarized in this review).
German population-based follow-up: 93% of young adults classified as dependent at baseline no longer were after about three years (von Sydow et al.; as summarized in this review).
US household surveys: about 4 in 100 past-year ecstasy-taking people met hallucinogen-dependence criteria (Stone et al.; Wu et al., 2008; as summarized in this review).

Australian sample of 1,662 regular ecstasy-taking people: 18% screened positive on the Severity of Dependence Scale; two correlated factors fitted better than one (Bruno et al.; as summarized in this review).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2010 summary of studies to 2009, usable as a second-hand description of what those studies measured. Later studies are not covered. Its main finding, that dependence-like problems are reported by a minority of people taking ecstasy but the evidence is limited in scope and design, has not been tested here against later work.

funding.funder: The Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing assisted the review; the first author holds an Australian NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (ID 510279); the acknowledgements also name the NHMRC. The funders had no role in the design, interpretation or write-up (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre (University of New South Wales), University of Tasmania and Justice Health (New South Wales). Two of the authors ran the two studies the review uses for the structure of dependence symptoms (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009), and 11 of the references have at least one of the three authors among their authors (editors' count).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people starting ecstasy, recruited from the general population rather than from services, with the content of what they take confirmed, a dependence instrument validated for MDMA and a clinician interview in a subsample, followed at repeated visits so that the share who become dependent, how long it lasts and what use pattern comes before it can be estimated with intervals, and compared with people using other drugs.

domains.note: Three databases and the search strings are given (footnote 1, p. 2), but there are no dates, inclusion or exclusion rules or counts, and the review does not say how studies were chosen for Table 1.

Section 3.6 states the main limits plainly (instruments from other drugs, self-report, lifetime recall, convenience samples), but studies are not appraised one by one and several figures differ between Table 1 and the text (Wu, Winstock, Bruno, Hanson and Luciana).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The structure of dependence rests on two studies by the authors (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009), and 11 of the references have at least one of the three authors among their authors.

The summary labels its own inferences with 'suggests' and calls for controlled studies (p. 8), but 'Human evidence supports this proposition' leans on the absence of case reports of severe withdrawal.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often dependence is reported
domains.note: The full range of figures is shown (3.6% to 73%) with the sampling frame beside each, and the text says the figures cannot be extrapolated to everyone taking ecstasy.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is candid about the limits of the human evidence and shows the range of figures with their sampling frames, so it can be cited as a second-hand description of what studies up to 2009 reported. It cannot be cited for how common dependence is in any group, because the figures come from different instruments, time windows and mostly self-selected samples. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but has dependence potential; some people report problems with their use, but physical features appear to play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance is apparent and withdrawal is self-reported, but it is unclear whether these reports distinguish after-effects of a session from a 'true' withdrawal syndrome; studies of structure suggest two factors, 'compulsive use' and 'escalating use'; a minority of people taking ecstasy become concerned about their use and seek treatment. Further controlled studies are called for.

Method and terms: searches in PubMed, PsycInfo and EMBASE with strings covering abuse, dependence, withdrawal, reward, reinforcement, ICD, DSM and nosology (footnote 1), with no dates or rules for inclusion. The authors use 'dependence' rather than 'addiction', following the two classification systems. No specific ecstasy or MDMA dependence diagnosis exists: a person taking ecstasy can be classed as dependent on hallucinogens and/or amphetamines, which differ in structure and in whether withdrawal is a criterion.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph and footnote 1 (search, terms); 1.2, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (classification)

key_findings.finding: Pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, and some or many may contain methamphetamine instead (citing Quinn et al., 2007 and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime), so dependence in people who take 'ecstasy' may be on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Studies that adjusted for other drug use, including methamphetamine, used self-reported use, not laboratory-verified use.

Animal work with pure MDMA: self-administration in mice, rats and non-human primates, so MDMA is rewarding; but substantial proportions of rats fail to acquire self-administration even after extended training, unlike cocaine, and the point at which animals stop working for MDMA is lower than for cocaine and methamphetamine. The review concludes that although MDMA is rewarding, it may be less rewarding than other illicit drugs, and that the course of dependence may differ from drugs such as opioids.
key_findings.locator: 2.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); closing paragraph of section 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Human evidence is thin: three case reports (Jansen, 1999) of two people with access to large amounts of high-purity MDMA and one with post-traumatic stress disorder, each with tolerance, increasing time using and recovering, neglect of other activities and mild withdrawal in the 'comedown', all three with other drug use disorders. Few studies have examined dependence; all used instruments first designed for other drugs, and only one (non-representative) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment.

Table 1, population-based and sentinel samples: US household surveys 3.8% past year (Stone, 1,199 people who started ecstasy within the previous two years, hallucinogen criteria; ecstasy more likely than LSD, peyote or psilocybin to lead to dependence) and 3.6% past year (Wu, 652; another 11% reported one or two symptoms); Germany 5.8% lifetime among those who had ever taken ecstasy (von Sydow, 207) with under 10% of those classified lifetime-dependent being past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up; 19% past year (Parsons, 214 New York nightclub attendees); 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, 200 Taiwanese juvenile detainees, amphetamine-dependence questions); Australia 18% past month (Bruno, 1,662 recruited by purposive and snowball sampling, scale cut-off 4 or more; among those screening positive 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month).
key_findings.note: Wu is 3.6% here and 4% in the text (p. 7); Bruno's monthly group is 1-2 times here and 1-3 times in the text (p. 7); Parsons gives 2.5 days over four months in the details column and 5 days over four weeks in the notes.

key_findings.finding: Table 1, self-selected samples: 43% lifetime (Cottler, 52 people in treatment services and the community; continued use despite problems 63%, withdrawal 59%); 14 of 26 students and community members met abuse or dependence criteria (Hanson and Luciana; prevalence cell reads 'N = 2 LT'); latent classes, no prevalence, mean 227 lifetime pills (Scheier, 639); 64% lifetime (Topp 1997, 185 Australians; at heaviest use 66% used 1-2 days a week and 25% 1-3 days a month; the authors questioned the withdrawal items); 16% (Tossman, 195 people who had taken ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year; 17% self-perceived dependence); 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, 154 Washington rave attendees, 'probable' dependence on a three-item screener); 73% lifetime (Thomasius, 59 rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794, clinician-rated SCID).

Table 1, last row: 17% (Winstock, 1,106 readers of a UK dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; Severity of Dependence Scale 5 or more; mean 160 lifetime occasions); tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Footnote a: timeframe for assessment not specified.

Text figures: past-year DSM-IV ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence among all young adults in Germany was 0.4% (von Sydow); 4% of past-year ecstasy-taking people in a US survey met hallucinogen-dependence criteria and 3.82% of those who had started in the previous two years had developed dependence (Wu; Stone); 17% of 154 Washington rave attendees and 16% of a German sample of current ecstasy-taking people were classed as dependent; Taiwanese detainees: 22% dependent and 36% with no dependence symptoms; in the Australian sample of 1,662, financial, legal and work-related harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common among those screening positive, independent of problematic methamphetamine use, and only 2% (n = 7) of those screening positive used ecstasy at least every second day.
key_findings.locator: 3.2, from the paragraph beginning 'Seventeen percent of 154 Washington rave attendees' to the end of the section
key_findings.note: In the Australian text the 2% is of the group screening positive.

key_findings.finding: Structure: ecstasy dependence criteria did not behave like a single factor as for alcohol, opioids, cocaine or amphetamine; Topp et al. (1997) and Bruno et al. (2009), both Australian studies by the review's authors, found two factors, 'compulsive use' and 'escalating use'. The review concludes that dependence on ecstasy may differ in nature from dependence on alcohol, opioids and amphetamine and that a separate category deserves consideration.

Course: the only study of prognosis (a German population-based study of young adults, mean follow-up just over three years) found that 93% of those meeting criteria at baseline were no longer dependent at follow-up; of that group 50% no longer used the drug at all, and of the 43% still using, most did not meet criteria for a use disorder; the authors suggested ecstasy dependence might be a 'transient phenomenon'.

Treatment: in Australia, ecstasy accounts for very small numbers of treatment episodes (under 1% of all episodes); in a Texas series of 38,350 treatment episodes between 1988 and 2003 for people admitted with problems with 'club drugs', club-drug clients had more problems at admission and more polydrug use than clients using alcohol or other drugs. The review says routine treatment data cannot be used to estimate treatment need, and that problematic use of ecstasy alone may be a less significant reason for entering treatment.

Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in how dependence was assessed and in the samples, making meta-analysis inappropriate; assessment was typically self-reported without clinician verification and by lifetime retrospective report; people very commonly reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as intended; prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people taking ecstasy because most studies recruited people who had recently taken ecstasy by convenience or snowball sampling; information on natural history comes from retrospective reports of convenience samples.

Summary: 'The evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is limited in both scope and design.' Tolerance and withdrawal rest largely on self-report in research studies using questionnaires designed for other drugs; there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal; some people clearly become concerned about their use; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use in the general population but do occur.
key_findings.locator: 4. Summary and implications, 1st, 2nd and last paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Winstock et al. (1,106 readers of a dance music magazine, 17%): Table 1 footnote a says the timeframe for assessment was not specified, and the text says the sample screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The window behind the 17% is not clear; it is not comparable with the past-year figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Wu et al.: Table 1 gives 3.6% past year and the text gives 4%; both describe DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence among past-year ecstasy-taking people, not an ecstasy-specific diagnosis. Stone et al. also used six items for hallucinogen criteria (Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two household-survey figures measure hallucinogen dependence in people who also took ecstasy, which is not the same as dependence on ecstasy; use the table's 3.6% and 3.8% and say so.

reporting_issues.issue: Bruno et al.: among people screening positive, Table 1 gives 34% using 1-2 times per month and the text gives 1-3 times per month; the text's 2% (n = 7) refers to those screening positive, not to the whole sample of 1,662.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small slip in a frequency band; the 2% must not be read as a share of all 1,662 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Hanson and Luciana: the prevalence cell in Table 1 reads 'N = 2 LT', while the details cell and the text say 14 of 26 met criteria for abuse or dependence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The row cannot be used as printed; 14 of 26 is also a sample of students and community members who used ecstasy, not a prevalence.

reporting_issues.issue: Tossman: Table 1 defines the sample as people who had taken ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year, with a footnote that the window was not specified; the text calls it 16% of people currently taking ecstasy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 16% may include dependence on methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Parsons et al.: the sample is defined by ecstasy use in the past four weeks, but the details column gives a median of 2.5 days in the past four months, and the notes column gives a median of 5 days in the past four weeks for the dependent group against 2 for the non-dependent group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency windows are not consistent; the 2.5 days cannot be taken as a typical weekly pattern.

reporting_issues.issue: Scheier et al.: Table 1 says latent-class groupings give no direct prevalence, but the text reports three groups with a greater than 50% probability of multiple symptoms and then '73%'; the same 73% is the prevalence printed for Thomasius et al. in Table 1, a study not discussed in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The highest prevalence in the table (73% of 59 heavy-using rave attendees) has no discussion in the text, and the 73% in the text paragraph is a different quantity.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 says two studies examined the structure of dependence, all involving Australian samples and one also including US samples, but the two studies described (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009) are both listed in Table 1 as Australian only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample behind the two-factor finding is not reliably described; the conclusion rests on two studies by the review's own authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary treats a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal as support for physical symptoms playing a limited role, although the review also reports that three case reports described mild withdrawal and that the literature is mostly survey self-report.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of case reports is not evidence of absence; the statement is an inference.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-10 (PDFs/MDMA/Degenhardt_2010_EcstasyDependence.pdf), full text including the funding statement and reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Table 1 (pp. 4-6, landscape and rotated pages) was checked row by row against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.
